blocks.text: Today you and the learner compare two fraction bars and decide which has more shaded.
The learner has met halves and quarters as equal parts of one whole.

blocks.say: One bar is split into halves, the other into quarters.
blocks.why: Seeing both at once makes the lengths easy to compare.

blocks.title: What only you can do
items: Watch which bar the learner looks at first.
Ask them to point before they say an answer.

blocks.title: A step ahead
blocks.body: If this feels easy, ask them to name each shaded part as a fraction.
blocks.prompt: What fraction is shaded on each bar?

blocks.q: What if they guess by colour, not length?
blocks.a: Cover the colour with a finger and compare how far each shaded part reaches.

more.q: What if the bars look the same length to them?
more.a: Line the shaded ends up with a straight edge.

more.q: What if they still are not sure?
more.a: Drop back to one bar and count the shaded parts out loud.

blocks.text: Note whether comparing by length or by counting parts worked better for this learner.

blocks.title: A step ahead
blocks.body: After you decide, try saying each shaded part as a fraction.

blocks.title: Two fraction bars
blocks.ask_learner: Which bar has more shaded — the first or the second?
blocks.why: Three quarters reaches further than one half, so the second bar has more shaded.

mistakes.half-bigger: Thinks a half is always more than quarters because its parts are bigger.
mistakes.more-parts: Thinks more parts always means more shaded.

items.q: One half and two quarters cover the same length. True or not?
items.explain: Two quarters join up to make one half.

blocks.q: How do I compare two bars?
blocks.a: Look at how far each shaded part reaches from the left.

more.q: What if they end at nearly the same place?
more.a: Use a straight edge to line up the shaded ends.

more.q: What if I am still stuck?
more.a: Count the shaded parts on each bar out loud.
